key_points.point: The document asserts that reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) acts as a mechanism to 'unlock' latent capabilities already present in large language models like GPT-3. By using a small fraction of compute relative to pretraining, the model learns to follow instructions without needing to acquire entirely new foundational knowledge. This supports the accelerationist view that scaling and subsequent fine-tuning can efficiently extract transformative utility from existing models. The document notes this process is limited by the model's pre-existing parameter space, suggesting that capability gains are bounded by the initial training phase.
key_points.verbatim: One way of thinking about this process is that it “unlocks” capabilities that GPT-3 already had, but were difficult to elicit through prompt engineering alone: this is because our training procedure has a limited ability to teach the model new capabilities relative to what is learned during pretraining, since it uses less than 2% of the compute and data relative to model pretraining.

key_points.point: The document argues for the rapid deployment of alignment research into commercial products to improve the utility of general-purpose AI systems. By moving alignment research from the lab to the API, the authors demonstrate a commitment to iterative product improvement. This aligns with accelerationist goals of bringing powerful AI tools to market as quickly as possible to solve user needs. The document acknowledges that this is only the beginning of a broader effort to refine these tools.
key_points.verbatim: This is the first time our alignment research, which we’ve been pursuing for several years, has been applied to our product.

key_points.point: The document supports the goal of creating language models that are more helpful and capable of following complex user instructions. By improving the model's ability to perform tasks, the authors aim to increase the practical value of AI for users. This reflects an accelerationist desire to maximize the utility and reach of AI systems. The document notes that this improvement does not come at the cost of existing academic NLP capabilities.
key_points.verbatim: At the same time, we show that we don’t have to compromise on GPT-3’s capabilities, as measured by our model’s performance on academic NLP evaluations.

key_points.point: The document proposes mixing original pretraining data into the fine-tuning process to mitigate the 'alignment tax' where models lose performance on general tasks. This strategy ensures that safety and alignment improvements do not degrade the model's overall intelligence or versatility. This is a key accelerationist intention: maintaining high performance while adding safety layers. The document highlights this as a simple but effective algorithmic change.
key_points.verbatim: We’ve found a simple algorithmic change that minimizes this alignment tax: during RL fine-tuning we mix in a small fraction of the original data used to train GPT-3, and train on this data using the normal log likelihood maximization.

key_points.point: The document claims that academic NLP datasets are not fully representative of how language models are used in practice by customers. By comparing InstructGPT to models like FLAN and T0, the authors argue that real-world API usage requires different alignment strategies. This supports the accelerationist belief that real-world deployment is the ultimate test of AI utility. The document suggests that focusing solely on academic benchmarks may lead to suboptimal real-world performance.
key_points.verbatim: Finally, we find that InstructGPT outputs are preferred to those from FLAN and T0 on our customer distribution. This indicates that the data used to train FLAN and T0, mostly academic NLP tasks, is not fully representative of how deployed language models are used in practice.

key_points.point: The document expresses a desire to continue pushing alignment research to create language tools that are safe and helpful to humans. This reflects an accelerationist commitment to ongoing R&D as the primary path to better AI. The authors explicitly state their intent to keep hiring and expanding this research. The document frames this as a long-term, iterative process.
key_points.verbatim: Our results show that these techniques are effective at significantly improving the alignment of general-purpose AI systems with human intentions. However, this is just the beginning: we will keep pushing these techniques to improve the alignment of our current and future models towards language tools that are safe and helpful to humans.

key_points.point: The document intends to use human feedback as a reward signal to fine-tune models, arguing that this is necessary because safety and alignment are complex and subjective. This approach prioritizes human preference over rigid, automated metrics. This aligns with accelerationist views that human-in-the-loop systems are the most effective way to scale AI utility. The document notes that this method is a powerful tool for improving reliability.
key_points.verbatim: We believe that fine-tuning language models with humans in the loop is a powerful tool for improving their safety and reliability, and we will continue to push in this direction.

key_points.point: The document asserts that InstructGPT models are significantly preferred by human labelers over GPT-3, even when GPT-3 is prompted to follow instructions. This empirical claim supports the effectiveness of the RLHF methodology. From an accelerationist perspective, this validates the strategy of using human-guided fine-tuning to improve model performance. The document notes that this preference holds across various model sizes.
key_points.verbatim: We find that InstructGPT models are significantly preferred on prompts submitted to both the InstructGPT and GPT-3 models on the API.

key_points.point: The document prioritizes the development of techniques to make models safer and more aligned with human intentions before widespread deployment. By using RLHF to reduce toxic outputs and hallucinations, the authors address immediate safety concerns. This aligns with the safetyist focus on mitigating harms through rigorous alignment research. The document acknowledges that these models are still far from fully safe.
key_points.verbatim: To make our models safer, more helpful, and more aligned, we use an existing technique called reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF).

key_points.point: The document acknowledges that language models can generate harmful, untruthful, or toxic content because they are trained to predict the next word rather than to follow user intent safely. This highlights the misalignment between raw model training and human safety requirements. From a safetyist perspective, this confirms that base models are inherently risky. The document uses this as a justification for the necessity of alignment research.
key_points.verbatim: But these models can also generate outputs that are untruthful, toxic, or reflect harmful sentiments. This is in part because GPT-3 is trained to predict the next word on a large dataset of Internet text, rather than to safely perform the language task that the user wants.

key_points.point: The document argues for the need to align models with the values of specific populations, noting that aligning to an 'average' labeler preference may not be desirable for minority groups. This reflects a safetyist concern for the societal impact of AI values. The authors suggest that inclusive processes are required to make these decisions. The document admits that this is a difficult societal challenge.
key_points.verbatim: More generally, aligning model outputs to the values of specific humans introduces difficult choices with societal implications, and ultimately we must establish responsible, inclusive processes for making these decisions.

key_points.point: The document asserts that complex human values cannot be fully captured by simple automatic metrics, necessitating human-in-the-loop feedback. This supports the safetyist belief that alignment is a subjective and complex problem that cannot be solved by math alone. The authors use this to justify the use of human labelers. The document notes that this is a core motivation for their research.
key_points.verbatim: This technique uses human preferences as a reward signal to fine-tune our models, which is important as the safety and alignment problems we are aiming to solve are complex and subjective, and aren’t fully captured by simple automatic metrics.

key_points.point: The document identifies the 'misuse' problem where models trained to follow instructions might also follow instructions to produce unsafe content. This is a critical safetyist concern regarding the dual-use nature of instruction-following models. The authors state that solving this is an important open research problem. The document emphasizes that safety depends on both model behavior and deployment practices.
key_points.verbatim: A byproduct of training our models to follow user instructions is that they may become more susceptible to misuse if instructed to produce unsafe outputs. Solving this requires our models to refuse certain instructions; doing this reliably is an important open research problem that we are excited to tackle.

key_points.point: The document supports the use of content filters and pre-deployment reviews to ensure the safety of the API. This reflects a safetyist desire for active oversight and risk mitigation in AI deployment. The authors argue that safety is not just about the model, but also about how it is deployed. The document notes that they will continue to monitor for misuse.
key_points.verbatim: But the safety of a machine learning system depends not only on the behavior of the underlying models, but also on how these models are deployed. To support the safety of our API, we will continue to review potential applications before they go live, provide content filters for detecting unsafe completions, and monitor for misuse.

key_points.point: The document admits that despite progress, InstructGPT models still generate toxic or biased outputs and make up facts. This empirical honesty is central to the safetyist perspective, which emphasizes the limitations of current alignment methods. The authors use this to frame their work as an ongoing, incomplete process. The document highlights the need for further research.
key_points.verbatim: Despite making significant progress, our InstructGPT models are far from fully aligned or fully safe; they still generate toxic or biased outputs, make up facts, and generate sexual and violent content without explicit prompting.

key_points.point: The document describes using human labelers to provide demonstrations and rank model outputs to train a reward model. The document notes that this is a multi-step process involving data collection and reinforcement learning.
key_points.verbatim: We first collect a dataset of human-written demonstrations on prompts submitted to our API, and use this to train our supervised learning baselines. Next, we collect a dataset of human-labeled comparisons between two model outputs on a larger set of API prompts.

This supports the skeptic concern that AI systems encode and amplify the biases of their training data and developers. The authors acknowledge this as a limitation that requires further research. The document suggests that this is a significant societal issue.
key_points.verbatim: Right now, InstructGPT is trained to follow instructions in English; thus, it is biased towards the cultural values of English-speaking people.

key_points.verbatim: It is also influenced by our customers and the preferences implicit in our API policies. We selected labelers who performed well on a screening test for aptitude in identifying and responding to sensitive prompts.
